candidates.attacker_control: The code query parameter is attacker-supplied. A signed client-session code can be obtained by the OAuth client that legitimately receives a victim's authorization code, or by another party that obtains such a code. The password-update endpoint requires only this signed code; it does not require a client secret, the victim's old password, or the password-reset key.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Confirmed that ClientSessionCode.parse checks the signed hash but not action/expiration, that ClientSessionCode.isValid is the only action/lifespan check in this path, and that updatePassword has no additional key, old-password, or client-authentication check. A normal OIDC code has the required attached user session. The main limitation is obtaining a valid code before it is consumed; after token exchange or other action changes, the hash may no longer match. No separate server-side check was found that would prevent the action-mismatch path.
candidates.impact: Unauthorized password change and account takeover for a victim whose signed client-session code can be obtained. The bypass also defeats the intended action and expiration restrictions on other login-actions flows, potentially allowing profile/email/TOTP changes without the corresponding required-action token. This crosses the OAuth-client-to-user-account trust boundary.
candidates.prerequisites: The victim must have authenticated so the client session has an attached UserSession and a signed code. The attacker must obtain that code before normal token exchange clears/changes the session action. The realm must permit the request over its configured SSL policy, and the user must have a writable local password credential. A code issued for CODE_TO_TOKEN or another action is enough for the action check to fail; the missing return then allows execution to continue.
candidates.root_cause: LoginActionsService.Checks.check records a security-failure response when ClientSessionCode.isValid(requiredAction) is false, but does not return false. Callers only inspect the boolean result, so they continue after an invalid action or expired code. In particular, updatePassword does not verify that the signed code was issued for UPDATE_PASSWORD or that it is unexpired, and it updates the account's password without requiring the old password or an action key. A normal OpenID Connect authorization code carries the user session and action CODE_TO_TOKEN, which is sufficient to reach the password-update code.
candidates.title: Invalid client-session action is accepted by password-update flow, enabling account takeover
candidates.trace: OpenIDConnect.authenticated sets clientSession.action to CODE_TO_TOKEN and emits a signed code in the redirect. ClientSessionCode.parse verifies the RSA-derived hash and loads the client session, but does not reject it based on action. LoginActionsService.Checks.check then calls ClientSessionCode.isValid(UPDATE_PASSWORD); that method returns false for CODE_TO_TOKEN or an expired timestamp, but check only stores a failure response and still returns true. updatePassword proceeds, obtains the victim UserModel from clientSession.getUserSession(), and calls updateCredential with the attacker-supplied new password. The same helper pattern also affects profile, TOTP, and email-verification actions.
candidates.unverified: Static review only; no runtime or test execution. I did not verify deployment-specific session persistence, OAuth code interception feasibility, or whether a particular realm/client configuration exposes a usable code. The source path is direct, but the candidate remains a lead rather than a runtime-confirmed exploit.

coverage_summary: get_source_scope reported 1,259 model-visible files, with no oversize, sensitive-name, or symlink exclusions and no binary skips in inspected searches. I reviewed security-relevant source across services (OIDC token/login/account/admin endpoints), SAML, adapter core, core JWT utilities, model JPA/Mongo, theme providers, LDAP federation, export/import, and server configuration. I did not read all 1,259 files line-by-line; templates and third-party library sources are largely absent or outside the useful review path.
limitations: No runtime, build, test, or exploit execution was performed; all findings are source-based leads.
External frameworks/libraries (PicketLink, RESTEasy, Undertow, Jackson, servlet container URI parsing) were not available for source inspection.
The selected candidate depends on obtaining a victim's signed client-session code before it is consumed; deployment-specific code exposure was not verified.
Some web templates and generated artifacts are not present in the visible source tree, limiting confirmation of rendered form behavior.
No source-relation index or patch/history data was available; text search and bounded file reading may have missed dynamically wired paths.

rejected_leads.lead: ClientCertificateResource.getKeyInfo returns the configured client private key without calling auth.requireView() (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/ClientCertificateResource.java:78-87).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible independent missing-authorization issue, but it requires any valid user bearer token plus a client for which a keypair was already generated. Not selected because the selected issue has a more direct account-takeover impact; this remains a secondary lead.

rejected_leads.lead: OpenIDConnectService.matchesRedirects treats a registered wildcard URI as a raw prefix (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/OpenIDConnectService.java:986-999), potentially allowing redirects such as a lookalike host after a registered wildcard.
rejected_leads.reason: Could enable open redirect or authorization-code theft, but requires a wildcard redirect configuration and was not selected over the login-actions authorization bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: ThemeResource/FolderTheme concatenate an attacker-supplied resource path without canonical-path containment (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/ThemeResource.java:42-54; forms/common-themes/src/main/java/org/keycloak/theme/FolderTheme.java:68-80).
rejected_leads.reason: Potential arbitrary file read, but exploitation depends on a configured folder theme and URI/path-normalization behavior outside the reviewed source. Lower confidence than the selected issue.

rejected_leads.lead: SocialResource.Checks.check has the same missing-false return after an invalid client-session action (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/SocialResource.java:251-272).
rejected_leads.reason: Same flaw class as the selected issue, but the immediate consequence is primarily redirecting into the social flow rather than the direct password-update path. Not selected.
Plausible authorization omission, but a useful attack requires a victim session identifier and the immediate impact is session deletion/denial of service rather than account takeover.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak 1.1.0-Alpha1 snapshot (1,259 model-visible files) with emphasis on authentication/authorization boundaries, OIDC/SAML, login and account actions, admin REST resources, adapters, persistence, themes, LDAP, and server configuration. The strongest source-level lead is a client-session action/expiry validation bypass in LoginActionsService that can reach the password-update handler. Several other plausible but more configuration-dependent or lower-impact issues were not selected.
